utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today we are Monday, the 27th of August, 2007. I would like to greet the representatives from the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused. I believe Mr. Coric is not in the courtroom today, and I hope he gets better very soon. We should resume our hearing by hearing a witness and his testimony. Prior to that I need to hand down a decision, and I shall give the floor to the registrar who has an IC number to give us, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Larry Forbes. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 642; the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 643; and the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number 644 with respect to Witness Antoon van der Grinten. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. This is the oral decision I shall read out slowly so there are no mistakes in the translation. This decision was handed down after Mr. Karnavas took the floor last week following statements made by an accused during a Status Conference. This Trial Chamber was not made aware of what Mr. Seselj might have said. Therefore, this Trial Chamber has no reason whatsoever to question the integrity of Mr. Karnavas and reckons that he is entirely capable of fulfilling his duties as Defence counsel to Mr. Prlic. Last Thursday in the transcript, line 23 of page 22145 [as interpreted], Mr. Karnavas spoke in very abusive language about Mr. Seselj. This Trial Chamber cannot accept this type of language, and according to Rule 45 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence warns him not to use such language again. The Trial Chamber orders that the particular passage in the transcript be redacted from the transcript according to Rules 54 and 81(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As this Trial Chamber, the Prlic Chamber has no authority over Seselj leaves the matter with the Seselj Trial Chamber who is fully competent in the matter and that Chamber can then take the necessary measures, the measures it will deem fit. So much for the tenor of this decision, which reminds all and everyone that the Trial Chamber does not question Mr. Karnavas's integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction I would like to make. It's page 21455, and not 2145.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I believe it's Rule 46 and not Rule 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And let me just state for the record when Mr. Seselj attacks lawyers, when he attacks Prosecutors, when he attacks members of the registry, it seems that the Trial Chamber or the Presiding Judges do nothing. They don't reprimand him. They don't cut his mic off. They don't do anything. So we're sitting here defenseless, and I understand that the two Judges or three Judges on the panel were not there, were not privy to the remarks that Mr. Seselj makes. However, you were the Presiding Judge in that hearing. You're also the Presiding Judge here. Ultimately, you have a vote to cast in this case. So if the Trial Chamber feels that I used language which I feel was quite appropriate in my description of Mr. Seselj because he is what exactly I claimed he is to be, then I suggest that the Trial Chamber in the future exercise its discretion which it has under the Rules to reprimand Mr. Seselj and cut him off whenever he is being abusive towards the rest of us. As I've noted, we, the Defence lawyers as everybody else, are not his punching bags and I know that Russia is behind him and therefore he feels entitled to say whatever he wishes, and this Trial Chamber or some other Trial Chamber may think that it's okay to let him go as he wishes, but I dare say all we're doing is aiding and abetting Mr. Seselj in his little game which he stated quite clearly on the record, and that is his intent to destroy the integrity of this Tribunal, this institution, and I don't think it's appropriate. However, I do take the Court's remarks seriously, and in the future I will restrain from using the language that I did use. However, I am unapologetic in my description of Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A small mistake on line 24. I believe it's -- it's 21455. To respond to what Mr. Karnavas has just said, the Trial Chamber in charge of the Seselj case will take the appropriate decision. This Trial Chamber wish to specify that as far as the upcoming witness is concerned, we have planned to hear him for two and a half hours. The Prosecution will have two and a half hours, and the Defence teams will have the same time. If, of course, the Prosecution oversteps that time, the Defence team will have extra time. As we have two days in which to hear this witness, we have some time ahead of us to discuss the issue of this witness. I would like to move into private session for a few minutes. I would like to have both parties' opinion on protective measures to be applied to a particular witness. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. If you can hear me, could you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marita Vihervuori, born 6th of January, 1943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which -- what job do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am -- I am a journalist. I'm writing for Finnish newspapers and also for Austrian press agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, have you already testified before an international court on the events which unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time you come to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to take the oath and read what is on the piece of paper which the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Just some information about the way in which this hearing will unfold over the next two days. We will be hearing your testimony today and tomorrow. You will first be asked to answer questions which will be put to you by the representative of the Prosecution, whom I'm sure you met today or yesterday, and after the first part of this proceeding -- of these proceedings the Defence counsel on the left-hand side, each representing one of the accused, there are six in all, will put questions to you. Sometimes the accused might put questions to you also. In addition, the four Judges before you can at any moment ask you questions, but we would rather put the questions to you right at the end or only during the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination of one of the parties if it is a burning issue. Then we feel that it is better to put the question straight away rather than waiting for the end of the examination-in-chief or cross-examination. If at any point in time you don't feel well, please don't hesitate to let us know so we can stop the hearing. We have a break every hour and a half so that you can have some rest but also to change over the audiotapes, because as you know, or maybe you don't know, this trial is being recorded and broadcast to the outside world. That is why there are six cameras in this courtroom. If at any point in time you would like to put a question to the Bench, please don't hesitate to do so. In very general terms this is how your testimony will unfold. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecutor, whom I would like to greet again, and I shall give him the floor right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everybody else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Madam, I would like to start with a few biographical details. Could you tell the Court what your academic background is?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I have degree in history and politics from University of Helsinki. In American terms, it would be Master of Arts. I don't know what is in European terms, but as it called Magister. And then I have studied after that in University of Munich, and also later half a year in University of Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court from what time or from when have you been working as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I have been working as a journalist actually all my life. Already in student time I was a redactor [phoen] -- it was student magazine which was the history students for all Finnish universities, but -- and then afterwards for day -- for several magazines, but I started to work for dailies - it means in news business - '87.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, from 1987, for which dailies have -- did you start working in 1987?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I started first for Aamulehti. It is the second biggest daily in Finland and is in Tampere, and then couple of months later in summer Turun Sanomat. Turun Sanomat is the third biggest newspaper in Finland, and printed in Turku. I also write now and then for Helsingin Sanomat, which is the biggest one in all Scandinavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, during the period before you started working for newspapers as a journalist, did you have occasion to travel within the Balkans or through the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I was first time in Yugoslavia personally '64, but my Yugoslavian friend was already before in Finland. Then after '64 I was still '73 every year in Yugoslavia and '73 I was even living there more than three months, but then afterwards between -- I started in daily and '73 Yugoslavia was me more a transit land and I was visiting of course my old friends but I was not any more studying it systematically like before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After 1987 when, if at all, did you start travelling to the Balkans again and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, then I was working for daily news, and from beginning of '88 till 2001, former Yugoslavia was my most important place to work because there was something happening all the time, and so I could say that there was some years when I was more in former Yugoslavia than Vienna. Only long break was in the time of Gulf War from middle of January till middle of April, I was in Amman, and in Damascus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in which year was that, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: 1991. Now, madam, did you ever write or publish any books as a result of your association with the former Yugoslavia or the territories of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. I have published about Yugoslavia you could say three books, or two and a half, how you will. I made a book in English translation. It is -- would be "Welcome to Hell," and it's really a thick book. It's big and more than 800 [indiscernible] pages, and it's telling the story what happened in Yugoslavia and why it happened. Then I wrote later, and it is even in -- published in German, the "Memoirs of My Dog". It's also political book and is also partly in Yugoslavia and telling this story from a little bit ironical point of view. And then third one what it could be told only half a book. I was taking part writing all the capitals of former Yugoslavian states for geographical book which is long series from -- I think it's originally French book, The Big LaRousse or something like that round the world and because there were -- because there was the whole Yugoslavia in that book, they ordered me to make these follower states and it was published in three languages; Finnish, Norwegian and Swedish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, during the period that we are going to focus on mainly during the course of your testimony it, that period is 1992 to -- through 1993. Could you give the Court an idea of the extent of your grasp of the political affairs and the political personalities involved within the former Yugoslavia or the territories comprising the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know all the personalities personally, but because I was following all the elections, all the so-called free elections, I had met many of these personalities. From the higher personalities I have been interviewing Milan Kucan, Franjo Tudjman twice, Ibrahim Rugova several times and been in press conferences with Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and so on, and but it's later only the Serbian politician I knew better was Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, just before proceeding, during this period I see in some of the documentation that we will be looking at that it seems that two people -- or that you had two colleagues with whom you travelled a lot during this period and the names are here. Marja --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mirja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- and Erich. Can you tell the Court who these people are.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mirja Kesavaara is a good friend of mine and she is photographing for me and she is also assisting me in many things because very often in news when there's something very hot news as in former Yugoslavia where I cannot divide my personality, so I could cover two things when I send her somewhere. And Erich Rathfelder is a German journalist who was writing -- he was redactor from Tageszeitung in Berlin first, but then later a free journalist who was writing of course to Tageszeitung, but several other German newspapers and also the Tagesanzeiger in Zurich.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the interest, is it correct that your dog Musti also travelled with you throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Not throughout this period because I'm not that crazy. But let's say that it happens now and then, a pet things that were not calculating. She was in Slovenian war because we were thinking it was an independence fire, and she was there in April 1990 -- April 1993, because we were actually originally bringing some aid to send to our Bosnia and we're already out of Bosnia when something happened and we had to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, madam, if we could turn back to June 1992, is it correct that you travelled to Mostar towards the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I know that Bosnian war was already older, but it was not possible to go to Bosnia because there was this occupied Serb territory surrounding it. So the first spot where -- where I could get was Mostar. It was also not very easy because Magistrale was broken you have to go over island of Pag and so. But I had gotten a message from -- that Mostar should be free from siege, and it was through and they told me that I was the first foreign journalist in Mostar after breaking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I see in the record that the transcript hasn't exactly captured what you said. If you say Mostar should be freed from who?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was surrounded from Serbs. It was a siege. It was the system in that war that towns were surrounded like Sarajevo or Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So when you arrived in Mostar, had it already been freed or liberated?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. It was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was the atmosphere that you encountered there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, the atmosphere was very many ruins, but everybody was friendly, released. There was nothing to eat, nothing to drink, but -- but what I noticed, for instance, I was in the Old Bridge and everywhere, and the Croats and the Bosniaks they were fighting with each other. They was in the centre even a graveyard where they were buried together. It was a very good atmosphere, a very released atmosphere. Of course, it was also sad because churches and mosques were not totally destroyed but full of holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if I could just clarify. You say the Croats and the Bosniaks they were fighting with each other.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Not against.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: With each other against --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Could you gauge the level of cooperation of the -- the relations between the Bosniaks and the Croats at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was good, and it was also in this some soldiers which I met. Anyway, one of them told that he was actually from Croatia, not a Bosnian Croat. It means that they all were fighting against Serbs, because at that time Serbs were the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to ask you in detail, but during the fall of 1992 or autumn, November, did you travel to Prozor and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps briefly tell the Court about this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to get to central Bosnia, and we went to -- and somebody told us that we should go through Mostar. We were in Posusje. There was one Croat who told me that we were making a suicide and told us we should go to Tomislavgrad. In Tomislavgrad -- near Tomislavgrad, we found a new road. Later, I heard from Mr. Prlic that Croat had been building it through the forest. It may be very true, but at that time UNPROFOR troops had been in Bosnia maybe one month and they were preparing that road because this road was later the main road with which the aid, humanitarian aid, was brought to Central Bosnia. Of course it was not -- not a motor road. It was a sand road, it was a narrow sand road through forest. But it was extremely important, and so we more than accident -- accidentally learned to know this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that "I heard from Mr. Prlic that Croat had been building it through the forest." When did you hear this from Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And on what occasion was that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: While I was making an interview and we were talking about the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back to that. Now, madam, Gornji Vakuf, did you also visit Gornji Vakuf during this period?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. And we get back from -- from Central Bosnia on the road to Central Bosnia, Gornji Vakuf had nothing special, but when we got back there was cattle market, and so the British Warrior tanks couldn't move because of cows and because of market life. It means that it was actually very normal in Gornji Vakuf at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This visit to Gornji Vakuf and to Prozor, this was prior to the announcement of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was all prior. It was all before. It was all before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your personal experience from what you observed during that period, what was your personal experience of the relations between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosniaks at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: They were very good. And it was a very important time. When we were in Split before we started, there was in the newspaper, I think it was Nedeljna Dalmacija, the title, "Turbe shall fall before the first snow is going -- going on the ground". And the first snow came when we were still in Posusje, it was a cold day. But we went there. And Turbe was very important place, because if Turbe had fallen, then Travnik, Vitez, and the road to Sarajevo would have been free for Serbs. So the Croats and the Muslims together -- or Bosniaks together, we were defending Turbe and they succeeded. They got so-called defence victory. Turbe didn't fall. We were living in Hotel Vitez, which was headquarters of HVO forces. We were visiting Turbe. There it was Bosniak who was leading us through the city, but a Croat drove us to Travnik. It means that there were -- it was very good cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this cooperation that you had observed which was good at that period, did you at any stage come to the conclusion or make an assessment that this cooperation was deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: What's deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Getting worse.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. No, not at that moment. Of course I knew there were radicals on both sides and somebody was making a Greater Serbia and somebody was dreaming of a Greater Croatia. And of course I knew in that time when I was actually in Syria and Jordan and Iraq, Tudjman and Milosevic had met in Karadjordjevo, it was '91, but this highest level was not to feel in the lower level where the people were defending their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know when the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was announced?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I suppose 2nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did this have any impact as far as you could see on the relations between Bosnian Croats and Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it was to see even if later the Bosnian Vice-Prime Minister Zlatko Lagumdzija that it was not meant ethnical but it was interpreted ethnical. When I saw the plan I knew at once that it shall be interpreted ethnically, and I think as far as I know from his story that it was based very much on that so-called Sporazum from Croatia which was made 1938, which never was get in power because the war and Hitler little bit mixed the cards, but anyway it based -- it was not based on census '91, and so it was very, well, positive paper for Croats, and it was not very good for Muslims. And Serbs, well, they had very much anyway under their control than Vance-Owen was promising them, so it was somehow in that paper already included that there shall come some quarrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I could refer you to Exhibit P 08 -- 8575. P 08575. And in the binder that's being given to you it's the second last document. Now, madam, if you could first turn to beyond the English translation the fifth page. That's the original version which appears to be in German.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, is this the article that you wrote, "The Croats are sitting on three chairs"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes it is, and I suppose I was writing it about sometimes in May 1993. This 5 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So we see a date in the top right-hand corner saying 27/5/95?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: But it cannot true. I have -- well, it -- it must be May '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Because if you read it, it's also told the Geneva negotiations they were beginning, 093.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. At the top, handwritten, it seems that this is for Frau Mag Schreiberhuber?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who is this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Hermine Schreiberhuber is the vice -- how you tell leader of foreign policy in Austria press agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Why did you direct this to her? Was this just the practice at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, no. I directed it to her so that it is not landing to rubbish basket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, I'd like to refer you to -- well, first if we can look on the first page of the English version in the first three paragraphs there is each time reference to an Ivan Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I never in my life have met Ivan Drnis. I was in -- several time in Tomislavgrad asking permission for that and that, and always I got it from office from Ivan Drnis with his signature. So I was thinking that the person who was giving it to me was Ivan Drnis, but he was not. He was the press officer of HVO in Tomislavgrad. He has also the name but I have forgotten it. And this fact was made clear first in one press conference in June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, if we can look at the third paragraph on page 1 of the English version. Well, third paragraph in the German version as well, and in this paragraph it says: "Already in January when the fighting flared up," and this is from that second line, "Drnis justified the Vance-Owen Plan. The world has given us these areas and so we will control them." Can you comment on this, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. It means that we were trying to get in Central Bosnia and we were telling after these experiences in November we were telling Mr. Drnis, "What are you doing now?" Because there was some fights between Croats and Muslims in Gornji Vakuf and some other areas already, I think in Busovaca and some other areas and we knew about them. We were not yet in Central Bosnia, where we were first under our way to Central Bosnia. That, "What are you doing? That -- your good brothers are fighting with each other." And answer was this: "The world gave these areas to us and we're going to control them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at the second paragraph, the paragraph just above the one we've looked at now, in here it's reported that Ivan Drnis listed areas the HVO wants to bring under its control, and then a little further down: "We have to think of the future, he answered when, we asked him if the power tags was the reason for the fighting in Jablanica. Jablanica provides Herzegovina as well as big parts of Dalmatia with electricity." Could you perhaps comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, in modern world, energy is one of the most important things for fighting, and in Jablanica there was artificial sea and power plant. It means that they wanted to control energy. And then because of certain nature of Bosnia, which is in different valleys, who is controlling the roads controls also Bosnia, and this only road which was at that time available it was in Croatian, in HVO hands. Of course, the Bosniak had also very many other roads but they were all in Serbian hands. So Bosnia was cut. And I think that this press officer which was not Drnis just told that they want to control the energy. They want to secure the energy because Jablanica was very important actually for Croatia. And of course this road which started in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the reference to Dalmatia or big parts of Dalmatia which also received electricity from this, Dalmatia, in what country does that lie?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: That's Croatia. It's Croatia. It's not Bosnian part but it's real Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you read any significance into the statement that, "We have to think of our future," and then it being coupled with power being supplied to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, when I went in January to Croatia, I noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I may interrupt. I think I'm going to object to the form of the question. If you look at paragraph number two, the Prosecutor correctly indicated that there was a quote, "We have to think of our future." Then if you read on, it appears that the journalist who also is testifying now as a historian and also as a military expert as well as an expert on energy, then seems to be injecting her own comments, her own interpretation and then later on, at the last sentence of that paragraph, says, "Herzegovina has to remain Croatia in any case." Nothing about what this gentleman said. It's pure, pure speculation on her part as to what the gentleman meant whoever he was that she attributed to be Drnis, "We have to think of our future." So I think the way the question was phrased is improper. It assumes facts not in evidence. I suggest that we take it one step at a time, we do it very carefully so we know what is this madam's interpretation of historical facts or military necessities versus what actually took place, keeping in mind we do not have -- we do not have as in the other interview, the tape or some kind of a transcription.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you heard what Defence counsel just said. When the person with whom you were speaking tells you, "We must think of our future," what you're telling us afterwards is basically just you speaking, or is it something that he actually told you? Is it you speaking? Are you adding something to what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if -- if you look in this article under the top, it's told analyse. It means that it's no interview. It's just a longer-term analyse what I made and I was quoting some -- some persons which were telling -- had told me some things, and this you can see with this points with the direct quotations, but it is an analyse of mine and I have never said that it's something else. It even says here in the paper that it is how I saw the things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on that, again, I would draw the Trial Chamber's attention to paragraph two. Based on that, I don't mean to be disputatious, you know, though I have been in the past, but if you look at it, and the journalist is perfectly entitled to analyse, but I think the way the question is phrased, and now the way some of the answers are coming, no fault of the witness, it would appear that it is this gentleman that she attributes to Drnis that is actually talking about the power plant, which then allows the Prosecution to later on draw the attention or draw the conclusion which he wishes for the Court that she is saying that during the interview Drnis is actually admitting that they're attacking these areas or the conflict regarding Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Vitez, Travnik, Busovaca, and so on and so forth are because of the energy. It seems that this journalist, who happens to have other knowledge of which she has not been qualified to testify about yet, but now we know that's her analysis, it's her spin, because obviously from this, the gentleman never answers her question and we don't have a tape so we don't know question, answer, question, answer. So I would appreciate, Your Honour, that if the Prosecutor is going to go down this line he do so in a very classical form. What was told to her so we know facts. Then if she wants to give an interpretation, that's -- that's a different -- and of course, I'll be objecting to that, but because the Trial Chamber can interpret. We want fact, fact, fact, fact, fact. That's what journalism is all about, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Kruger, you heard Mr. Karnavas and the answer of the journalist. Now, what's important to find the truth with a capital "T" is not so much her analysis of what the person said, it's what the person actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, I won't belabour this point because I think it is of less importance in the bigger scheme of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll step off this document, Madam, but we will be getting back to it at later stage to just touch on perhaps one or two further aspects. Now, after the entry into force of -- sorry. After the introduction or announcement of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, did you again visit Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. I started actually this time my trip from Banja Luka and Krajina, and then I had to go back to Croatia, and then I visited second time Central Bosnia, and it was not that easy any more than before, because even they told that hostilities were not any more there. There was some -- not only some, very much shooting in Gornji Vakuf, and we have to drive through Gornji Vakuf. We have to wait on the edge and then we were -- and then the British Warriors were securing the road and then we have to drive so fast as we only do in these streets full of grenade holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And while in Central Bosnia at this time did you try to interview or did you interview any of the leadership figures?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. And this time the most important persons I was first interviewing -- well, February. I don't know. I think in February -- yeah, January, I didn't meet -- not very important. I think the most important person was the commandant in Mostar. I think his name was Kulenovic. Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia did you try to interview Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, I tried, but I didn't get him. Oh, yes. The important person at the -- you mean, I suppose is Dario Kordic, but I couldn't take him so seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Dario Kordic, when you interviewed him, madam, how did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, he was introduced to us as vice-president of Herceg-Bosna and as a colonel, but as far as I knew, he was student of politics in University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, from your interview with him were you able to gain any picture of his relationship to the leadership of the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I, of course, don't have any DNA, but anyway it was told that he should be the son of the sister of Mate Boban. It means from the president of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And other that that do you know if he had any links not of a familial but more in his work procedure or --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, he must have mentioned Mr. Prlic, because in my story --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Now she's speculating. "He must have mentioned." Either he did or he did not. Now, if she wishes to consult her notes - I assume you have notes from those days - I have no objection to her consulting those notes which of course I'll be requesting, but otherwise I would appreciate if she does not speculate as to what somebody might or might not have. That's not proper journalism. You know, I know it and the Trial Chamber knows it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, you've heard the objection, but from --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Because in my article is that he is near Prlic. So he has mentioned this name because it was to me not familiar, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage you -- can you remember any further details round what you have just said or is this basically --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, what was for me important in that interview was that he was threatening to cut the road to Tuzla. It had already been cut and they were quite desperate in Tuzla because we visited that only -- that also. But it was just the normal talk of securing -- securing this and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, let's step on to a different topic. Are you aware of talk of an ultimatum that was issued by the HVO early in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It should have been 3rd of April, and about it there was several press reports in Austrian press, and I suppose also in English press, Reuters and so on. It means that it was -- it was not my thing. I was reading it like any consumant [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I may refer you to Exhibit P 01804. And this is the very first exhibit in the bundle you have. It's the very first document in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I think, madam, you still have the --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: That's Borba. The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you just --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Oh, still one. Okay. Yes, yes, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. Madam, this is titled with the headline "Bosnian Croats demand Muslim troop pullouts," dated April 4, 1993. And just above that it's copyright 1993, Reuters Limited, the Reuter Library Report. As a journalist, are you able to tell us what the Reuter Library Report was or what this kind of document represents?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, somebody from Reuters has had knowledge about this -- this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Excuse me. Your Honour, at this point I would object to the witness testifying about this particular document unless there's a foundation laid. Obviously she did not pen this particular article, and unless it can be demonstrated that somehow she had access to this, read it at the time, I would object to any question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me make my record and you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just make my record. So unless, unless she was aware of this article at the time, I would object. Now, the question came prior to this with respect to an ultimatum. He can ask about that particular issue. But to try to get the witness to authenticate what somebody else wrote about something else is improper unless some sort of a foundation is laid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, I'm sure you have a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, there is a reason, and my next question will show that the objection was an utter waste of time of this Court, and if I'm just given the time to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we look at this document, I'm going to just point out one or two aspects of it and then I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. I object unless the foundation is laid. Was the witness aware of this article? If not, there's no need to look at this article because we're going to have this witness commenting about what another journalist wrote. That was the purpose of my objection which was not a waste of time. Perhaps the gentleman could kindly laid lay a foundation, if he's capable of doing that, and I dare say he's not, because the witness has not seen this document before, at least not during that period of time. And if she has, I'm sure she would have volunteered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has testified that she saw reports of this nature in the Austrian press and I would just wish to ask her whether what is in this press report corresponds in basis to what she saw in the Austrian press. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, this article, if we look at the body, the very first paragraph says: "Bosnian Croats on Sunday demanded the withdrawal of Muslim troops from provinces designated for Croat self-rule under a UN peace plan, reviving tensions between nominal civil war allies who battled early this year." And if we go further down, one, two, three, four -- about the fourth paragraph down below that: "The HVO set an April 15 deadline for Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic to sign a joint communique ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if we go two paragraphs down from that "If Izetbegovic fails to sign this agreement by April 15, the HVO will unilaterally enforce its jurisdiction in cantons three, eight, and 10. The statement from HVO headquarters in south-west Croat stronghold in Mostar warned." Now, madam, you had mentioned that you saw reports of an ultimatum in the Austrian press.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How does that accord to what we've just seen here?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it's about the same, because the system is working like that. Every newspaper and, for instance, Austrian press agency, they have Reuters. They are just translating it, and if they choose something it goes to whole Austrian press, but I don't have access to Reuters. I have access to Austrian press agency and I buy every day several Austrian newspapers but they were all writing about the same -- this can be the original -- original one. I don't know, because Austrian press notes not "Reuters," they make a note "agencies".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, following the objection of Defence Counsel Karnavas, when you saw the Austrian press I would like you to tell us whether upon reading these articles in the Austrian press you formed an opinion that was close to what you can see here in the text of the Reuters agency. Did it say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it said the same thing, but -- well, if you are following some country, if you are covering some country, you just read everything what is -- what is written about it, and of course when I went shortly after that to Bosnia I was asking about this ultimatum, is it true or is it not true, but the knowledge originally I got only through the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we could look at the next document in the bundle, which is P 01808. And if we can actually look at the original, a photocopy of something coming from Borba. My first question to you is: Do you know or had you heard of Borba or what it was?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I believe that it was a Serbian newspaper from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, on this page next to the picture of a man with his hand held on his head, there's a short article and that's the one that has been translated. In the English it stands, "HVO ultimatum demands pull-out of Muslim troops from three provinces." And the agency that is listed is Reuters. My question to you is you have seen this article yesterday, and it appears as if this would -- or may I ask you, from your experience with the Austrian press agency, if the Austrian press agency puts out a report, how is that report used by other publications?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: They have cooperation with other news agencies. I don't know how -- I think -- well, there are -- I think almost all small agencies belong to it. How much they use the material or each other, I don't know, but very many of my articles which I wrote to Austrian press agency were also in the Swiss one, and now and then even in DPA. It means that the news agencies, especially the small ones, they are cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if they use something coming from the Austrian press agency, would that be indicated in the article in another newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: In Austrian newspapers, yes, and if it's coming from the Swiss STA, they put their own sign there and it's used from Swiss newspapers, because my articles have been in Swiss newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just a final question on this. If another publication or newspaper uses something attributable to the Austrian press association, may they abbreviate an article and use only parts, a portion of the report?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, yes. That's the problem with the news agencies; it's only material. They can change it, and they are very often making it so they have the same thing from different agencies. It means made, of course, from different persons and they put them together and take this view from there and that from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, I'm asking you as a journalist this article in Borba, which is attributable to Reuters, it appears as if it uses --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Non-leading question, please. Non-leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, could you comment on the similarity between this article from Borba and the previous article we saw from Reuters.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, they are very similar, but it don't mean that they are the same article. If it has been, for instance, some press conference it could be that hundred people are writing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, madam. Let's step off from this topic. Now, in April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, please, before we move on to another subject. Witness, the Prosecution is asking you questions about a document which was published on April 5th in Borba, but the Prosecution did not ask you to look closely at that document. Now, if you would please do so as I do. I am noticing that the Reuters paper actually refers to two sources of its own. There is the HVO press release from Mostar, but also the Croatian radio station. So Reuters adds two elements to the document that we saw dated April 4th. There are two new sources. One HVO press release from Mostar and something that was said on the Croatian radio. Did you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, when there are different sources, you as a journalist, would you say that these different sources -- the fact that there are several sources, does that confirm an information or does that make it less reliable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, honest answer is very difficult. It's depending. Let's say when we have, for instance, a press conference which is pure propaganda, so it's all the same if there are hundred journalists which are writing the same propaganda. But there are two sources. It's a Croatian radio, and it is in that case actually good source, and there is the HVO General Staff. Because these sources are both Croatian ones, it makes it, in my opinion, reliable because if it would be a Muslim source then I wouldn't trust that much, but now I'm thinking future, because in the future then Croats, they were saying it never was an ultimatum but here is a document which are based on Croat sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, did you know another journalist by the name of Ed Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I didn't know him very well, but we all knew each other which were going and coming in Bosnia. Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you meet him in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I met him in press office in Split and he was sending his articles. He was just came from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, we talked shortly. He only knows that in Bosnia has happened awful things and he also know that in Mostar there had been fighting in former day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What did you do, if anything, as a result of your conversation with Ed Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, because we had already met a Bosnian journalist who was also telling that there has been happening awful things in Central Bosnia, we decided to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Apart from what Ed Vulliamy had told you, that awful things are happening, did you have any other details of what this might be?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, where did you specifically want to go? If you say, We wanted to go to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, first we got, of course, to Posusje and then it was always -- it had to be to get some permissions. And then to Mostar, because it was not necessary to go to Mostar if you want to go to Central Bosnia, because the road went from Tomislavgrad, but because Vulliamy mentioned that in Mostar had been fighting, we wanted to go to Mostar to see what was happening there because it was the next point to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And where did you go to in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, first we were driving around a little bit and we noticed that it was pretty normal. Coffee houses were open, but on the river it was dangerous and the most dangerous place was the Old Bridge. So it was actually on a little bit behind. It was normal and then we went to the headquarters of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, just before we proceed, if you say, "We went to the headquarters," who is "we" at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: We are the three persons which I already mentioned, Mirja Kesavaara as my photographer, and Erich Rathfelder as my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you remember where the headquarters of the HVO was?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: But anyway, in Western Mostar, of course, somewhere central.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What did you find when you were at the headquarters? Did you speaker to anybody?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I suppose that we went -- I don't have to suppose. As a journalist you go as -- first to the press officer, and press officer led us to the -- promised to organise us -- us an interview from higher level and brought us to the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Where they were eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: We were a while in canteen and we were looking. We were very astonished because there were soldiers in black uniforms and we were asking what are these and they told only that they are special troops but they didn't tell us what was their speciality. Later I heard from other journalists that their speciality was to -- to cleanse Muslims from the rows of HVO and put them to prison camps, because before, before in 1992 and a little bit later it was so that in HVO were fighting very many Bosniaks also, because it was the time when they were best friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can just backtrack one moment. When in April was this? Can you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure from the date. It -- I know that -- that in the papers there are told 22nd, but it can be as well 24th. And why? Because I can tell you something. It was the day in which the United Nations Security Council visited Ahmici. It was the same day. So it's very easy to check if it was 22nd or 24th. Why I'm telling 24th is while I was writing my articles, 25th, and they were all published 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go into this in detail, but you mentioned at line 10 of page 37: "Later I heard from other journalists..." and then you described certain things. Which other journalists are you referring to? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No, sorry that's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You said you had learned something from other journalists.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I can't mention the names because there were always pretty many of them, and you were talking. But there was at that time plenty of British journalists, so I would say from British journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you try to confirm or check the information that this journalist had given you regarding the soldiers in black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. At that moment I didn't have any possibility or, let's say, I didn't have time to check it and I was at that time not so interested in this black -- black uniforms, but it was later when it was told, and if it's true or not I cannot tell, but I can tell that -- that Muslims disappeared from HVO and there were afterwards prison camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one question to ask perhaps before the break, or if you -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, just going back very briefly to something that you had mentioned earlier. You mentioned at some stage Sporazum in 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: '38, sorry, 1938. Can you perhaps give the Court some more detail on this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If it's going to take too long, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No, it won't take too long. Let's say so that Yugoslavia, the first Yugoslavia, there was a certain quarrel between Serbs and Croats because it was a unitarian state without any -- it was no federal state, and there was a quarrel. There was a murder. The Croatian parliamentarians was murdered, '27, and Yugoslavian king was murdered from Croats, '34, and so on and so on and so sometimes they decided that let's make an agreement and give -- so that it shall be peace in this country, and it happened, '38. Croat got better position at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Are you sure, madam, are you sure it wasn't the Sporazum of 26 August 1939? That is the date I have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you have so exact date then it is, because even I'm an historian I don't remember everything by heart, but I have always believed that it was already '38. But anyway, it was this Sporazum where the quarrel between Serbs and Croats was finished. And there was a certain area given to the Croats where they have a kind of -- should have a kind of autonomy but it was never in power because a certain Hitler attacked Yugoslavia and it was involved in krieg -- in war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can break, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. A 20-minute break. See you here again at 16.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Vihervuori, just before the break -- shortly before the break you mentioned that in the HVO headquarters in Mostar you were taken to a canteen by the press officer and you were asked to wait. Had you asked at that stage to -- for an interview with any specific person?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What happened when you were then in the -- in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: We were sitting there and waiting, and as usual Erich was trying to make conversation with everybody. I'm not that communicative. And then somebody came and told that we get an interview and led us to a villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This person who told you about the interview, was this the press officer you had spoken to previously?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he say with whom this interview was going to be?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. He told that it would be with Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you know who Jadranko Prlic was at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. But he gave -- but it was told me who he is, and he gave also his card, so I knew -- I knew. I just -- what I didn't know was that what is behind this card, because I was always thinking that HVO, that it would be on the top actually only a general, and -- and the name of the general, how -- it was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I don't remember that now at that stage, but I know who is the commandant, the military commandant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, when you find out who Jadranko Prlic was, before you arrived at this villa or at the villa?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: In the villa. Or in the garden of the villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This villa, do you know where it was?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't find it, but it was in Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was it a residence or an office?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I would say both. Anyway, the room we were it was an office, but it was such a beautiful old villa. Surely somebody has been living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you say that Jadranko Prlic gave you his card. I'd like you to look at the very last exhibit in your bundle, which is Exhibit 9063. P 09063. And if you look at the second page of that, that's a photocopy. Do you recognise this photocopy or what it is?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It is the copy of that card.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know where the original of this card is?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, in my pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Here in court. You still have it?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. But -- so the point that I wish to ask you is on giving you this card did Mr. Prlic tell you what his function was or what position he occupied?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. It was already told. I mean, it's also in the card. President of Croatian Defence Council. So it means that it is a kind of political leader from Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Vihervuori --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Or maybe -- maybe you could also tell defence minister. I don't know how the titles were in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the interview with Mr. Prlic, how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It last 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who were present during this interview?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: He and Mirja Kesavaara and Erich Rathfelder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: And I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In what language was this interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Directly in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how was this -- the contents of the interview recorded?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I was making notes. I have my own system to make notes. In my green years I was making tapes, but I noticed that it's very slowly way. If you're in news business, it's better to make notes. Of course Erich was taking a tape. Of course if I would have known that I am some day going to sit here I would have taken my tape recorder, but I was never dreaming of that, so I was just making a normal interview for newspapers with notes with some sentences which are direct quotations which I need and then some indicates about other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Before coming to the substance of the interview itself, did you write any newspaper reports or articles subsequent to this interview based on your notes?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. And also based on these notes was this investigation which the two investigators from here in October 2001 were discussing in Vienna. I had these notes in my hand. Also, this investigation was based on these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And subsequently what has happened to these notes?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I don't know. They are somewhere, but I have hundreds of logs from every interview, so -- because I was investigated 2001, and I didn't think I'm very important, so I didn't give very much attention to it any more because I thought that I won't come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And prior to coming here to testify, did you look to see if you could find these notes?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, but unfortunately I was cleaning last year my old three writing tables. I didn't clean them to waste basket, but to archive, and archive is also a very bad place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kruger, may I ask a little question on the notes. In which language did you take the notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Finnish language. That's why I didn't give very much attention to them, because in my handwriting and in Finnish language, you need an Egyptologue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Now, in the statement you gave to the investigators, you mentioned that the tape, and I take it that this refers to the tape made by Erich Rathfelder, had gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I didn't -- well, maybe I said something like that. I was telling that Erich was recording this, but I suppose that it's lost because he had in his working room hundreds of tapes. It was to me a very big surprise that you found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, madam, you said -- we found it yesterday. I played it tape to you, and did you recognise it when this tape was played to you? First of all, did I play the whole tape?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No, you didn't play the whole tape, but you bring that much that I could recognise my voice and Erich's voice and a third voice which has to be Mr. Prlic. It's 14 years ago, so I don't remember his voice by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to Exhibit 2046. Exhibit 2046. And we see here that this says "Interview made by Erich Rathfelder and Marita Vihervuori with Jadranko Prlic in April 1993." Madam, have you had the opportunity of reading this document?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It is not the interview. It is not all it have because there are always these points, and then as always it's nothing exceptional. After somebody -- after the tape recorder is closed there shall be a little bit discussion still, and so the end of the interview or the last sentences they are not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before proceeding, Your Honour, if I may mention at this stage for the benefit of the Court and for the benefit of the Defence, the actual tape is available electronically if anybody wants any portion played in court. It is also fully synchronised with both the B/C/S as well as with the English transcripts, but unless the Court determines otherwise, I do not propose to play it, but we'll just work on the basis of the transcript for my further questions regarding this. Now, madam, in the course of the interview -- or perhaps if -- if I can refer you to the first page of the transcript, and just above the middle where there's "MV ..." Just above that, that paragraph, in the middle of that paragraph, and this appears to be JP, which I take is stands for Jadranko Prlic, he states: "... I think that, and it is my opinion, official opinion, that this fighting is -- cause of this fighting is attack of Muslim troops to HVO troops at Croat people in middle Bosnia." Could you comment on this and what you discussed regarding the cause of the conflict in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we have any commenting or analysis from our good journalist, perhaps a foundation can be laid. We have the tape. We were provided with the tape. We couldn't hear anything, so we assume that over the years something had happened to it, but that's another story. But be that as it may, we have a transcript. The Judges can read the transcript. Now, if we're going to be asking for the witness to give a spin to the transcript, I think a foundation needs to be laid first before any such questions, otherwise I would suggest that the transcript itself and the tape itself are the best evidence, and as such it is the transcript and the tape itself or the tape actually is the best evidence, that is controlling as opposed to what the witness wishes to spin on. Now, again if she wants to give an analysis she has to -- we need to have a foundation laid by the gentleman, which at this point in time no foundation has been laid as a predicate for the question which he just asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, at the time when this interview took place, how familiar were you with the situation in Herzegovina and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, not -- I was not aware of the acute situation. I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina some days before. It was in the beginning of April we were there, and I was discussing with various leaders, for instance with-- with commandant of 3rd Army Corps of Bosnian army, Hadzihasanovic, which later he was chief of the staff. And I was also discussing with Ejup Dautovic, which was the imam of Zenica, but it was about raped women. It has nothing to do with it. I know that there was a big tension because we had again difficulties to get through Gornji Vakuf, but what had happened after that when I got to Croatia from Central Bosnia I didn't know. I knew only what the Bosnian journalists and Ed Vulliamy had told me, that something awful has happened, and then I could think what this awful was because of what I had seen in January, February, and what I have seen in the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And regarding the things that Jadranko Prlic told you during the course of this interview, were you in a position to be able to comprehend what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we know what "things" mean? "Things" are a lot of things. Anything from what he ate to what his function was to what was happening on the ground. So what are we talking about "things"? If we could have a precise question. The question is broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is broad because it's very clear what the transcript is about. The purpose is, first of all, to just assess generally what the -- what the witness's level of -- or competence was to understand and interpret what Mr. Prlic was saying at that stage, whether she was able to independently assess whether this was indeed correct or not from her own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In that event, Your Honour, he can simply go about it by asking who, what, where, why, how, explain it, describe. For instance, what exactly did you know about what events were happening in and about Central Bosnia. Then she can give her narration. That's how to do it as opposed to either leading or ask an over-broad question, because then a statement -- an article is written thereafter where in the article the journalist, as most journalists do, also put a spin to it trying to interpret whether the narrator was actually true, accurate, correct or what have you, in this case he was sticky sweet or however you want to describe him. I think we can go step-by-step. And if Mr. Kruger needs some help, I'll be more than happy to conduct his direct for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid wasting any time, Mr. Kruger, if you would like to address the issue of Mr. Prlic's questions, you need to ask the witness how she prepared herself for the interview. Did she walk into it and, in other words, what is the situation as things stand, and the journalist then asks, And in Konjic, and you could have asked her why she put the question about Konjic and then continue with your series of questions. Because there are some questions which she puts which we don't figure in the document because they are small dots and Mr. Prlic's answers and we don't have the question. And so if you wish to highlight a number of important points of the interview, then put the question to her and say you put such-and-such a question and what was your reason for asking the question. Otherwise Mr. Karnavas will object and waste the court's time and everyone has understood what the Chamber is interested in, namely Mr. Prlic's answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we can actually turn to something which we have dealt with previously in the course of -- of this afternoon. If we can go, and this is again on the first page, and right at the bottom you ask -- or there is a discussion about an ultimatum. Now, can you tell the Court why this came up and why there was a discussion about this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it's very clear. Firstly, I had, as I already told, read about this ultimatum. Secondly, I was asking Hadzihasanovic what the Muslims are going to do, and I suppose I was interviewing Hadzihasanovic on 13th of April because my interview was published on 14th. And Hadzihasanovic told that they are -- that they don't believe that something happens. They didn't take it seriously. Then I was by Prlic, and I had the knowledge from -- from my colleagues that something very bad had happened, and so I was just counting one plus one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, we see in this interview that -- and this is the last paragraph on the first page, that Mr. Prlic says: "There are only one proposal." And if we go further down, the third last line on that page: "Mr. Boban sent proposal about it. It was on the 3rd of April. There are no any terms in it proposal." How did you understand this in -- in light of your knowledge of the ultimatum of the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking, but I don't know if my thoughts are important, that he's lying. That -- because there was a knowledge about this ultimatum. I had it from the press. I had it from Bosnia. And there was this line everywhere told, and he tells, "I don't know anything about it." So I must tell that Croatian leader was very badly informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, did you discuss this during the course of this interview?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No, we were not actually discussing it, but -- but it was many times mentioned that there was mentioned about these -- these sections which should be Croat, and there was -- there was discussing about that, that -- well, no problems with -- with multi-ethnical provinces and so on. It was -- it was all the time there, but Vance-Owen Plan as such was not under discuss. I mean, it was in discussing in that these regions were mentioned, and Mr. Prlic was of the opinion that it is a good basement for Bosnian peace and so on, but we were not arguing about that document, if it's good or bad or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, if we look at page 3 of this transcript, and it is the -- you can say the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us that when you met Mr. Prlic you'd had an interview prior to that with Hadzihasanovic. At the end of those questions you put to Mr. Prlic, did you put them to him after those questions you had put to Hadzihasanovic? Was it in the light of those questions you'd first put that you put these questions to Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was interviewing Hadzihasanovic about 13th of April, and Mr. Prlic about 10 days later. And I knew that between had had happened something, so -- so I was somehow -- I was not thinking Hadzihasanovic at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you tell Mr. Prlic that you had met Mr. Hadzihasanovic before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic at some point, on page 2, says that you had information from one side only, and more specifically when you talk about Gornji Vakuf, you mentioned that the artillery at Gornji Vakuf had been displaced. So you are putting a question to Mr. Prlic on military matters, and he tells you -- in other words, he contradicts what you are saying. Why didn't you tell him at that point that you had information on the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because I didn't have this information from 3rd Corps. I had this information from -- from near the Gornji Vakuf and also from BritBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that when you put questions to Mr. Prlic, you are not going into the interview blindly. You already had information at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had some informations, but I didn't have informations from the acute situation.
