When I was discussing with Hadzihasanovic, the topic was mostly the common leadership of Croatian and Bosnian -- I mean, Croatian, Bosnian, and Muslim Croatian army and how the difference is going, how the cooperation is going because of these incidents which happened in the beginning of the year, and Hadzihasanovic was very, very positive. It means that when I was ask -- interviewing with Prlic, Hadzihasanovic was to me an optimist who has totally miscalculated the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Kruger. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, just to -- for the clarity of the record, this interview -- you've actually already mentioned it, but was it a planned interview or a spur of the moment kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: With Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was -- well, we wanted to talk somebody in -- in Mostar because we knew -- because we knew that there had happened something and we were going round, but I didn't ask a certain person. I was very astonished that we got so easily to so high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, the -- or the original audio version of the tape is quite bad, and that is why there are lots of dots or spaces in the transcript. If we turn to page 3 of the transcript, the second place from the top where you ask a question and where there are only dots, just below that Jadranko Prlic starts answering: "Mr. Bartolomio visited Mostar before two weeks." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this discussion is still about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. About three lines down, Mr. Prlic says: "We want to stop the war and the Vance-Owen Plan is probably the only solution of existing of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Without Vance-Owen, there are no Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you recall perhaps your question or what triggered this discussion or response?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. No. And what is, if I may so, funny in this paper is that I have been so much speaking and Erich so little. I don't remember that he had problem throat at that day. Normally it was so that Erich was talking mostly. So I think that quality of record is that bad that even Erich's questions are made in my mouth. But I know this. We were discussing about -- about existing of Bosnia and that kind of things. But what I should have been asking, after 14 years I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, if we can turn to page 5. And if we can look at the very last paragraph. Now, once again the question is not clear, but the question triggers the response from Mr. Prlic that: "Our aim is not to go with Croatia." And then it follows on: "... We want to have whole Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina is our state." Could you explain to the Court what this means?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. Why would the witness -- she can explain what she thought Mr. Prlic meant and gives -- but I don't understand the basis for the question. It is what it is. I mean, Mr. Prlic made that statement. Now, what she interpreted that to be, because maybe she has, you know, some suspicion which would then trigger some sort of follow-up question, that's fine, but -- and again, I want to point to the Court's attention the following: She's going to be writing an interview or writing an article based on this interview. She is not some official -- or there in some sort of an official capacity such as some international, for instance, where thereafter she's going to react in accordance with answers that she's going to be getting from this particular individual because of his position, but I believe the way the question is being asked is totally improper. Now, if he wishes to rephrase it as to what she thought he meant, which then would cause a reaction from me as to speculation, because now she's going to be speculating as to what exactly Mr. Prlic meant at that time since she didn't have access to his brain. So I don't see the purpose of the question, but I'll wait for clarification, but at this point I'm going to be objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just briefly respond. The -- I will rephrase that question, but the witness is a professional journalist who was in the area, and as a professional journalist certainly she did have the competence to at least assess what was being told to her at various stages and then to also find or point out or comment on certain inconsistencies within what was being told to her, and this is the -- where I'm aiming at with the following questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kruger. Witness, so that the Bench is able to understand everything about this interview, you said you didn't know who Mr. Prlic was, and you discover who this person was at the last minute because you hasn't prepared your interview with him in mind. Also, there's something ambiguous about this interview. You said so yourself. On the other hand there are you and your colleague. You are asking the questions. And in English the -- the name of your colleague is not mentioned. The initials MV are in the document, but you said that your colleague did ask questions. So we don't know whether Mr. Prlic's answers are answers to the questions you put or to the questions your colleague put to him. Was this a red thread in your interview? Usually a journalist has something of a -- did you have something of a common thread, something which you were preparing beforehand? Because usually when one interviews an important person you know what kind of questions you are going to be putting beforehand. Did you know in which direction your interview was going to go or was it just open questions you were putting to him based on information provided to you by BritBat or other -- from other sources which you were basing your interview on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. There are different kinds of interviews. One is a very good prepared with ready questions, and the other one is a discussion, and this was more a discussion. And many, many times when we were making common interviews, Erich and I, we made already before clear that you ask that, I ask that, and so on. It was -- it is all the same who was making the questions, because it was -- anyway, we worked very goodly together. And to this last capital, in that state I can even recall my question which is not there, because Mr. Prlic is in the previous -- he was, and that I remember because they are the important thing, telling that he's Croat, not Bosnian Croat, that he's -- that Yugoslavia was better than Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on. So my question was: "Are you going to join Croatia?" And the answer is: "No, that's not our proposal."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, what you are referring to is on page 5, the second-last paragraph just above MV; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, something which I want to ask you how you understood this at the time as a journalist when it was told to you is in that same paragraph, the third line from the bottom -- well, before that, from the second line: "You know, I want to say something. For Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Yugoslavia is better than a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why? Because Croatia was in that Yugoslavia. Now there is border to Croatia. You know, Yugoslavia was a complex country and now BiH is not a complex country. It would be a unitary country." Now, during the interview what was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: There was some -- a certain contradiction. On the other hand, Mr. Prlic was speaking about no problems with the multi-ethnical state, and on the other hand he was telling that it's not a good state for Croats. Yugoslavia was better. What can I think in that moment? I was thinking of Serbs and Milosevic. And I was thinking, of course, this Karadjordjevo and these plans of dividing Yugoslavia, which were mostly Milosevic initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, on the next page, at the top, just beneath "Side two," in the light of what you've just said, Jadranko Prlic says: "You know, Croatian nation and Serbian nation is homogen nations. There are no big differences between Serb in BiH and Serbs in Serbia. There are no big difference between Croat in Croatia and Croats in Herzegovina. We think that real Croatia is Western Herzegovina, for instance." Now, at the time when this was said in this interview, how did you view this in -- in terms of what had been said previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, if he could just read the entire question or the entire answer and then ask her, because you have to put it in context. And keep in mind they're both speaking a second language of their own, but at least let's have the whole thing and then I don't object to that question. She can have whatever impression she wishes. But the whole answer because it puts it into context, because I think it's the very last sentence that drives the point home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we read the whole thing, then, it goes further: "I think that in a global sense one possibility to solve the situation is negotiations between Croats and Serbs. But I know that ... to agree on any agreement about the situation in BiH which not included all three nations in BiH." It seems that there may then be something missing from the transcript. Which then prompted a question which ends with: "You and Serbian side want to destroy Muslim nation." Can you recall what your -- what your understanding of this statement was at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it was the discussion about -- the old discussion about dividing Bosnia, and the problem was that Serbs had Serbia and Croats had also Croatia, but Muslims, they didn't have anything. They had only Bosnia. And everybody was thinking that they are weak. So it's very easy. Just divide Bosnia and to kick Muslims out. Because I think it was about that. It was exactly same mistake what Serbs made in -- in Croatia. They were thinking that Croatia should be very soon crushed, but the Croats were fighting with bare hands to defend their homes. And couple of years later, after Dayton treaties, Mr. Prlic told Erich and that's secondhand, but anyway, I trust Erich, but they were thinking --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, madam. I will object at this point because now we're talking about beyond Dayton and Erich isn't here so this is beyond the scope of the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, hearsay is admissible and this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I never said that it wasn't. I understand hearsay, even hearsay on hearsay is relevant, provided it can be backed up by independent indicia. That's not the point. I well familiar with the rules of evidence. What the point is, is now we're talking about what she heard or somebody heard after the Dayton Accords. It has nothing to do with this particular interview. We're talking about 1997, Dayton being in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Kruger, this is an interview that is before the Dayton agreements, so there's no point in bringing up Dayton. What interests the Bench is the questions placed by madam and her colleague and the answers given by Prlic at that time, that is April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, what -- I'll just come back to what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on the question that Mr. Kruger just brought up, at some time you or your colleague asked Mr. Prlic the following question: "You and the Serbs are trying to destroy the Muslim nation." And Mr. Prlic answers you: "Why?" At that time we don't know exactly what you're saying, and Mr. Prlic is giving an explanation. He's saying that during the six months when the UNPROFOR was there, there were, et cetera, et cetera, but what -- what this means is Mr. Prlic's answer does not fit in with the feelings that you or your colleague were voicing about the destruction of the Muslim nation. Do you remember that particular time in the interview, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is two levels. The one level is political level, and the other level is -- is that humanitarian level. And so when I'm asking political questions about possible dividing from Bosnia or something like that, he is answering how much Croats had been helping Muslims before UNPROFOR came, because UNPROFOR came first in October '92. And all these refugees were brought to Croatia before it. And that's all true. But it has nothing to do with these questions I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is that his answer was just an attempt to steer the conversation away from the question that you posed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how can it be then that you did not choose to steer him back towards that subject afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that our time was closing, because it's in the very end of -- of an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, if we can turn to page 4 in the transcript. And if we look at the third paragraph where Jadranko Prlic gives a response, that's the one starting with: "I think that it depend on which you speak -- on which who you speak, you conversate." That paragraph. We'll look in a moment at the contents, but at this stage had you any idea of the ethnic composition or the statistics regarding ethnic composition within Bosnia and Herceg -- Herzegovina at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, every journalist had the map of the census of Yugoslavia '91. Everybody knew. That was an official paper. You could get it everywhere. So you could -- and there was told exactly how many from which nation in which town were living. But at that stage you could only know that in the Serbian-occupated area -- but not occupated but the area which was under Serbian control there were very many Muslims and Croats expelled and where they were it was not know. Partly they were in Central Bosnia, and partly they were outside Bosnia and partly even outside Yugoslavia. It means that in the situation from ethnical cleansing which had been the fact already since -- since the war begin -- begun in April 1992, in the beginning especially in Serbian-hold areas. Nobody could exactly told how many refugees are sitting in which town, but I'm not counting the refugees population because it was also possible that they went go further or they can go back. But the ethnical composition from every town was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look in that paragraph, the fourth line, it says, "... Croats make ethnic cleansing of Croats." From there downwards, Mr. Prlic says, "The number of Croats will decrease in all of this period and in the future also. We had only 17.5 per cent of Croats before the war in BiH. Today, not more than 12 per cent ... In this situation we will be national minority in BiH." Now, this statement of the Croats becoming less and who will eventually become a minority, was this something that you had heard before or heard subsequent to this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, yes, but in other context. I heard dozens of times in -- in Kosovo, when the Kosovo Serbian leaders were singing how the number of Serbs are -- are getting less and less and they are only 7 per cent, Momo Trajkovic, and that's why they have to kick some Albanians out and so on and -- and I was thinking in Kosovo at that moment it means that for me it was a kind of excuse of a nationalistic fears. We are getting less. We have to defend our positions. If the Croats really get less in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can say yes, in numbers, but if they got less in -- in comparison, I don't know because refugees were still more than Muslim nation. I think that the number of refugees was very high at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at page 2 of this transcript, the last paragraph on page 2. And if we look at the fifth line of that paragraph: "There are less number of Croats in Bosnian provinces than before the war. There are more Muslims in Croat provinces than before the war." Were you in a position at that stage to -- to understand whether that was accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was true. It was true in that meaning, that so many Muslims were ethnically cleansed. There were enormous refugee camps, for instance in Posusje, at that moment. Well, I think he was thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was this a sort of concern to the people you spoke to within HVO circles?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No, because it was maybe excuse for something, but nobody was concerned about refugee camps because they cannot stay forever. They were very, very bad camps. They were cold, there was nothing to eat, and the situation was bad. It doesn't mean that if you have refugees that it should be a lasting thing or lasting situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we can turn to page 5 of this transcript and the paragraph about in the middle of the page where Jadranko Prlic starts: "Logic is not always." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In that paragraph the discussion turns to -- to the HVO army, and Mr. Prlic, in the middle says: First point that was the Muslim army and the Croat army don't have a good relationship. The second point: "We have a huge army. It is greater than Croat army in Croatia." And then he refers to: "At the same time we don't have more than 20 previous officers, not more than 20." Did you understand what he was referring to about 20 previous officers?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. He was meaning in HVO were only 20 officers which were serving in JNA, in former Yugoslavian army, and telling that in Bosnian army were several former officers from former Yugoslavian army. If it's true or not, I cannot tell it, but I know that many commanders in all armies had been before serving in JNA because it was -- they wouldn't have had any other military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, Mr. Prlic, when he spoke to you about the HVO, the military, and then in the rest of this transcript where he speaks about the implementation or not of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, et cetera, did you -- did you form an impression at that moment as to whether this was a person who was speaking from a basis of authority?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From what did you gain that impression?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: He was one of the highest leaders in -- in -- in the Bosnian Croat or in Herceg-Bosna, which was already at that time founded, and it correspond -- corresponded. I don't know, and nobody knows how near the contacts were to Zagreb. That I don't know. And how much authority, for instance, Mr. Tudjman had to these things, because we cannot call Tudjman here. He's dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, you say that after the tape was switched off there was still another part to the interview, and you referred to a meeting between Mr. Boban and Radovan Karadzic. Did you tell what that discussion was about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we have an answer to that question, it's indicated, at least today we learn for the first time, sometime late in the morning, that the witness has indicated that something was said to her after the tape recorder was turned off. It wasn't mentioned when she was interviewed. It wasn't mentioned in her statement. It wasn't -- there's a reference to this point in what she wrote, but she makes some sort of a notion that this was from her shorthand notes. We've heard today that those notes are unavailable. They may be in her archive, albeit it's probably not terribly well organised from what I understand, but if there are going to be any answers to this part, I'm entitled to have all of that, because if she's relying on those particular notes which only she has had access to, then I would move to disallow any questions concerning what she may or may not remember at this point in time because we don't have access to that information. We have access to a tape, one that was provided to us that we could not hear anything, which of course we'll be moving to get a cleaner copy. We have the transcript from the tape, but we do not have her notes, and I am at a distinct disadvantage at this point because I have to take the witness at her word and I choose not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I have been listening to Mr. Karnavas with some attention. Now, you told us that you were taking notes - that's the way you worked - in Finnish. So I presume you asked a question. You asked Mr. Prlic a question, he gives you an answer, and on your piece of paper you note Mr. Prlic's answer. Now, the tape is off. The tape player is turned off. Now, it seems that the conversation was going on after that. Now, when the conversation was still carrying on with Mr. Prlic, did you, on your notebook at the time, note the questions that you carried on asking, and did you also note the answers that you were getting from Mr. Prlic on subjects that do not appear on the piece of paper that we already have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I note the answer. I didn't note my question. And I have many pieces of paper where this answer is. It is in my book. It is in the press articles which I was writing on base of my notes at that time. At that time it means one day after this interview. So if you want, I can bring you my book and my press articles which are based directly on these notes. They are not in that meaning disappeared because they were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So everything you are -- that you mentioned to Mr. Kruger, these elements that do not appear on the tape or on the transcript of the tape, everything is based on notes that were in fact used for the books that you published and for the articles that you wrote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And actually it wasn't very much. The only important thing was that he admitted that Boban had been visiting Pale to get trust -- because it was necessary to get just trust solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So you are telling us that Mr. Prlic told you that Mr. Boban had had gone to Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And this, Mr. Kruger, is what you would like to use as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if -- if I can immediately request the witness to turn to Exhibit 2094. Exhibit 2094.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if you can turn to the German version, the original. And this is a document titled "Genozid in Mittel Bosnia," and at the top Mag Schreiberhuber. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: That is my original article, and if you look in the very end of it you see that -- that I have been writing it on 25th -- 25th of April. That is the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In the English version that is on page 6 of the translation. Now, madam, can you tell us, this article written on the 25th, I see it's titled, "The interview with the HVO president in Mostar." Which interview are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: This interview. What we are discussing all the time. The interview with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, the contents of and the factual contents of this article, where did you obtain the material for the factual content?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it -- it was my notes from the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the second page of the English translation, the English version. And if we look at the very second paragraph. It says: "Prlic does not deny that Boban would have met secretly with Radovan Karadzic." And: "According to his statement, it is necessary to talk with the Serbs ..." And it goes on. At what stage did Mr. Prlic say this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was in the very end. I think we were already standing and shaking hands. It was in the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it was maybe already in Erich's bag or pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you recall the context in which this final part of this discussion took place, or what generated this information from Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was the discussion about the future of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to find a solution, because nobody wants a war. And -- and -- well, of course it is said very beautifully here in the interview, but in the fact it was to me actually dividing up Bosnia, because, funnily, Serbs were not very active at that time when Croat and Muslims were fighting, because Croats were doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the first page of the English transcript, or it's the very first paragraph of the original version if you wanted to look at that. And it says -- it starts off the article: "The president of the HVO, Jadranko Prlic, is as sweet as sugar. He denies any violation of human rights by Croats against Muslims in Central Bosnia and repeats the official propaganda according to which the Croats are victims." Now, this appears to be your own assessment of the -- of the interview with Mr. Prlic. What made you come to this conclusion and made you write this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, when I was writing this it was next day from the interview, and my information states what's totally different as by the interview. I had between visited with the UN Security Council representatives, for instance, Ahmici. I had saw the burnt villages. I had been discussing with many officers of BritBat. So I was at that time when I was making this article, I was very well-informed, informed of the situation. The previous day was so full of programme that I never came to write. I made all what I had seen and heard in the next day, first in the next day in shelling as is told in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in what manner did the fact that you visited Ahmici and that there was a United Nations Security Council delegation also visiting Ahmici? How did that change your information basis?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I saw what happened. For that I have only second-hand, and that's for historian. It's not very good evidence, second-hand information. But then I had first-hand knowledge. I had my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- Ahmici, did that at all come -- or the events that occur at Ahmici on 16 April 1993, had that all come up during the course of the interview with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: By the course of interview with Mr. Prlic I had never heard the name Ahmici. I was asking from the British major, information major with -- who was coming to my car, I was driving him there, and asked, "What is the name of this village? Can you spell it to me?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The fact that a United Nations Security Council delegation was visiting Ahmici, did that all come up in the course of the interview with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know it. I -- I was told when we got to Central Bosnia -- we were told, "Sit here." We were sitting in the car and waiting for something. We didn't know what we were waiting. Then suddenly they told us, "Now let's go." And we were joined to a long convoy. I was thinking what is this crusade now, where we are going. And suddenly we went the one destroyed village, and for us was the commandant Bob Stewart of the BritBat, Colonel Bob Stewart, and four representatives of the United Nations Security Council. We learned that first in Ahmici that that -- that something like that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, when you came across this delegation from the United Nations Security Council, first of all, did you know who was leading this delegation?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- I don't remember his name, but it was the guy from Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And my second question on this: Were you able to ascertain whether the HVO authorities were in any way involved in setting up or arranging or allowing this visit by this delegation?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think that it was organised from BritBat because there was no representative of HVO. I think that they didn't especially like that UN Security Council came to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, if we can change to page 2 again of the article, and this is the second section which talks about the street blockade of Tomislavgrad. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now the very first paragraph and this refers to -- is in relation to Tomislavgrad and it says that, "At the street blockade, stood a line of UNHCR lorries of several kilometres. Our press passes were also not accepted. The name Prlic was not considered authoritative." Can you comment on this? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: We were told there was free access of goods and persons, but in Tomislavgrad nothing was going on, just nothing, but what was very odd was that we were sent three times to get some paper to -- because there is some kilometres between this road blockade and Tomislavgrad. Maybe 25, I don't know exactly. We had to drive three times to Tomislavgrad. Nobody took the responsibility of letting us through, and nobody took the responsibility of preventing us. But anyway, this -- that everything was so free and wonderful as we were told was not true. It was to see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just the next paragraph. You -- along the same line it seems, "'He is their president,' said a high British officer for him. This was another proof that local Croat units were not under control." Can you comment on this, what you meant when you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well I'm quoting an angry British major. They were -- they were very angry because in negotiation level it was guaranteed that they can get through, but in the reality they were -- they were not let through and the humanitarian help was also standing -- standing there. And because it was systematical preventing and closing Bosnia, it was actually using blockade as a weapon. But, of course, nobody is admitting such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, if we can turn to page 5 of the English version. And if we can look at the second-last paragraph on that page. It's the one that starts with "Ahmici is also ethnically cleansed." You have that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, what's interesting in this is from the second line: "For Croatia's reputation, the occurrences in Central Bosnia mean a tremendous loss. Herzegovina Croats started with a genocide at exactly the same time as the Croat President Franjo Tudjman was visiting the USA to commemorate another genocide. The behaviour of the Herzegovina Croats is a burden for Croatia." Can you recall on what basis you wrote this, what caused you to write this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, firstly I was thinking on the visit of UN Security Council, and in that context Bob Stewart, the British colonel, was telling that it was a systematical genocide. It started everywhere at the same point. It was -- his words was: "It was not an obeyance from lower level. It was from high leaded." And on the other hand I was thinking because shortly before Tudjman had been in America, I suppose in New York, and remembering the genocide on Jews, because there was also some concentration camps in -- in Croatia in the time of the war, and Croatia had, because of Ante Pavelic, a little bit fascistic reputation. And so Tudjman was trying to repair that reputation and at the same time happens this kind of genocide in Central Bosnia. It all didn't come together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, just the next paragraph. We've touched upon this previously, but this is basically an assessment of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. "The Serbs have not subscribed to the Vance-Owen Plan because they have already conquered far more than the plan awards them." And then, "The Croats couldn't wait to sign as the plan awarded them more than they had dreamed of." Is this your own assessment or was this generally spoken about --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: That was generally spoken. The Serbs had 65 per cent of Bosnia under their control, and -- and for Croats this paper gave very much. They were happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, the very last sentence of that paragraph: "They tried to push through -- this refers to the Croats, "They tried to push through their interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan with force." Was this your assessment or was this generally spoken about at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was generally spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, "generally spoken". What does that mean? Who are these generally spoken -- who are these people so we can cross-examine? We have this particular witness, it is her assessment. Is it her assessment? And based on what? That's the issue over here. And that's not -- hearsay can come in but who are these hearsayers? I think it's improper and I think it's unprofessional to ask questions in this fashion, and I would think Mr. Kruger would know better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, when you say that that was generally spoken, we are reading your article so that you are speaking. You don't say in the article some people say or it is generally said that. You are making your own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I'm making my conclusions, but I'm also discussing with my colleagues. Well, let's say "generally spoken" maybe in that so-called journalist [indiscernible]. I didn't have very much other contacts in Central Bosnia than the victims and the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we can jump to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute. If we're going to move to another subject with Mr. Kruger and now that I have the paper in front of me, I do have two very brief questions for you. Your article was published in German under the general title, "Genocide in Central Bosnia." Now, that is a very attractive title. It's going to draw lots of attention. Now, looking at the text more closely, I note on page 4 in the English version that a Russian member of the Security Council told you, on the subject of Ahmici, that this was not genocide. Wouldn't you say that there is a contradiction between your title and what is actually inside the article? There is a paragraph in which you are discussing, apparently with a member of the Security Council, of the delegation that was present there, and they obviously didn't actually say that it was a genocide. And in fact you are quoting Vitez, where 200 more people apparently had been killed. Why then did you choose to call that article genocide if only to quote an interview of the HVO president in Mostar where, as we saw earlier in the interview, there's not much about genocide in the content of that interview? Could you perhaps say a few words to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, this article was never published in this form. This is the original material which I was giving for Austria Press Agency. It was there little bit more beautifully written, without grammatical mistakes and so on. But I was thinking this what I have myself have written is authentic. But I don't think that it is with this title anyway. My title in Finland was "A Death of a Village" in my Finnish article. That I know. That is first thing. Secondly, the Venezuelan guy told quite publicly that this is genocide and this must be published -- punished. And also in Austria, this is all the material what I was giving them on that day. There were four different or maybe five different messages, UN agency messages. An agency message never looks like that. That is the material what I gave Austria press agency that they can make it in that form what they want, and the press agency is always very serious media. They don't have titles like yellow press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for these clarifications. It makes it easier to understand. The title of the article was not then yours. You actually called it "Death of a village."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In Finnish article, I called it, "Death of a Village". What I made in Austrian, well, it was all the same because I knew that they anyway make their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Vihervuori, jumping to another topic. Did you know a person by the name of Veso Vegar?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: He was the pressman of HVO in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When did you meet this person?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Autumn 1993. I -- I don't know. October or November. I was pretty long time at that time in -- around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how did this discussion come about? Under what circumstances did it take place?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: In press office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you recall who was present?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, the same. The same as before. I, Erich Rathfelder, and Mirja Kesavaara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was the main topic of discussion with Mr. Vegar?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: The situation in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you talk about -- at all about detention centres or prisons?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. We were talking very much about prisons, because it was a topic which Erich Rathfelder always wanted to talk, and Mr. Vegar was telling us that they are going in the next future, in few days, close the prison camp of Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Had you heard of Gabela at that stage or did you know about Gabela?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I knew that there are some prison camps. I knew from name Gabela and Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before continuing with Mr. Vegar's discussion, did you, subsequent to the discussion with Mr. Vegar, talk to anybody else about Gabela shortly after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: What Mr. Vegar was talking, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No. But did you talk to anybody else about Gabela?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I was not talking -- talking anybody else, but I went from Mostar to Medjugorje. I was normally living in Medjugorje because Mostar was divided town with shootings and so on. And in Medjugorje I met two mercenaries -- or three mercenaries, or let's say they were not quite real ones because they didn't like the war. They learnt it very soon that it's better to not. And one of these mercenaries had had a long beard, and so Croats were thinking that he's a Chetnik and arrested him and sent them to Gabela. That's why when we met he had quite white face because he had shaved himself for security. And he told something about Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When was this? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I suppose it was on the same day as Mr. Vegar or in the next one, but they were very close to each other. And that's why I was asking him that -- that Vegar told that it shall be closed, and he don't know because they just brought new weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one further question on exactly this topic, but I see it's 25 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, just one more question. I think you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, this mercenary, did he say anything about what he had encountered in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: He told that the people were starving, that the food was not to be eaten. He told that he didn't see any bodies, but he see -- but he saw -- saw coffins, and these coffins were loaded to -- to a truck, brought back, and then again brought away and then again back. So he made the conclusion that the bodies were -- that they were full of bodies and they were taken to some mass grave and the coffins were used several times. And then he telled -- and it was very funny when I was asking how much people there are, he said 1.500 plus 25 plus 1. These 25 were persons which were taken, according to him, from fields directly to Gabela and one of them was very old and in very bad shape and he was thinking that he won't survive and he told that they had been mishandled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who was the one?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was he.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Because he didn't count himself because he was only three days. So he was plus one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We will now take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, upon commencement if I may just for the record state that with regard to Exhibit 02046, that is the audio recording of the interview with Mr. Prlic, during the break the Prosecution has made available to all Defence counsel and to Registry then also with additional copy for the Bench. We have made available the cleaned-up version, hopefully which is a little bit better quality of the audio recording of the interview, and we hope that's consistent with everyone. The audio recording and the transcript, I have checked that they do accord to each other. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you were referring to your conversation with a mercenary who had been in Gabela. Can you recall the name of the mercenary?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: No. And the mercenaries very seldom told their names. There are some I know the name, but because he was so exact and because of his dialect and his way of acting he was in my eyes like a former officer, officer from DDR, Stasi. So he's in my notes just with the name Stasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can return to your conversation with Mr. Veso Vegar. Now, you mentioned that the main topic of the discussion was Mostar when you spoke to Mr. Vegar.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about Mostar were you talking if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, in Mostar, the situation was in Mostar at that time very bad. We were actually hanging in Medjugorje to get in Eastern Mostar which was totally seized. It was a pocket. And Mr. Vegar told that "Anyway, they," it means Herceg-Bosna, "has to get Mostar for their capital," and he was telling why. "Because it's the only town we have." Maybe he meant bigger town. The others were so small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If he says, "the only town we have," what do you understand him to mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Herceg-Bosna HVO. Bosnian Croats -- I mean Herzegovina Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he take you through Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Not he personally, but we made a very funny walking. Somebody was sending us always to places but not coming himself. "Go there. Go there." And then -- but there was nothing to see. But then Erich noticed that we are always on the plain place where we could see from Eastern Mostar, and well, maybe they wanted that Bosniaks shoot us when we were walking there, but they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, now you were in Mostar at various stages during 1992, 1993, and 1994. You mentioned that you were in Mostar in July 1992 just after it had been liberated from the Serbs, and then you were there, as you stated now, towards the end of 1993. Can you perhaps give the Court just an idea of the levels of destruction in the city as you observed it from July 1992 and then in -- towards the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: The difference was not very big, and I cannot compare it, because 1992, after liberation, I was on the bridge. I was on the bazaar area. It means I was in the old centre, which is mainly inhabited from Bosniaks or it was a bazaar. But that time when it was divided we didn't get in Eastern Mostar. The Spanish UNPROFOR promised it several times but it never came true. So I didn't have any possibility to see what was the situation in Eastern Mostar. Western Mostar was not very destroyed. I saw the situation in Eastern Mostar first when Croats and Muslims made their federal state, and then it was pretty destroyed, but it was, I think, first in the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you went there.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: In the eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you, during 1993 and 1994, ever go to Pocitelj?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And when did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was one of my trips to Mostar. It was after the federation was made. It is 1994 or 1995. I suppose 1994. But anyway, it was at that stage when there were no hostilities between Croats and Bosniaks, more they had their common state. Herceg-Bosna was not officially -- was still officially in -- live but there was already this peace between these two nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Under whose control was Pocitelj when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Had you been in Pocitelj before that time?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, because it was a kind of museum village. It was a very beautiful museum, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: A museum in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was old Bosnian, I mean Muslim, culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- what did you find when you were there in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it was a little bit destructed, and we wanted to take photos, and we stopped and there was one man, armed man sitting in a coffee house and stand up and talk that if we are taking one photo, he'll shoot us. Well, we didn't take the photo. We disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This armed man do you know from what military organisation he was?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I'm not sure but there are only two possibilities, HVO or some paramilitarian, but in that place HVO is more likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You say the village "was a little built destructed." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, it was not totally in ruins but the mosques were and how you call them Koran schools and what all kind of things in the Muslim culture they are. They were hit. They were not totally abolished. It was not that kind of destruction what the Serbs were making when they were making asphalt and parking place instead of old mosque. They were just ruins.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you around this time also visit Gradsko?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes. Only -- only once, and it was twice, actually, but it was very unhealthy visit. They didn't like that we take photos from mosques, but what we were doing, we were trying to find the people of this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before going on, if I may interrupt you, where was this village?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was near Medjugorje. If you come to Medjugorje from coast so it's on the left side, little bit before when you turn right to Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, you say once again "we" tried to find the people. "We", who --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was the same, let's say, group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you said "they" didn't like that we take photos. Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: They were HVO. It was also very unhealthy, but I think we got a couple of photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you find out what had happened to the people who had lived there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Actually, not very surely. We were looking them from Red Cross. Red Cross didn't know. We were looking them from UNHCR. No, they didn't know. Somebody wrote that maybe they are in some Croatian refugee camp, but we didn't find them there. And then later, much later, it was already the war was over and there was WEU police, and I suddenly met a Finnish policeman there, and I asked him, Can you find me these people of this village, and some months later he called me and told that -- that his contact persons have told him that they were -- they were killed and that they are in some kind of mass grave in -- in a forest, but he told me that don't go to look after it because they are full of mines. But if it's true or not, but I must tell that the person who was looking for me, this -- this refugees is a policeman, and nowadays he's the one who is studying the place where crime has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you wanted to take a picture of the mosque. In what condition was the mosque in this village?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It was exploded. It means that -- and it was very funnily exploded. Funny is a wrong word. It was exploded so that there has been a kind of bomb inside, so that the walls were like, in German, swollen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Swollen.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Swollen. And some rips, long holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Tears.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just a few final things. Madam, during 1992 and -- to 1994, were you able or in a position to follow what was being reported in the Croatian media, either newspapers or television?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes, when I was on Croatian side I was always listening the news, and I was trying to read the newspapers. I could understand some Croatian. Now I haven't been there many, many years now it's very rusted, but I could understand the main things. And I could understand the line in which they were going. Not every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to assess the -- the position that was being given or given through the media regarding the conflict between the Muslims and the Bosnian Croats during that period?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, ma'am. Excuse me. Objection, Your Honour. Who is "they"? Through which media? Okay. She's talking about being able to figure out what's happening in the media, but who is "they". Are we saying now there is -- are these the official media or are these interviews? If we can have more precision perhaps I may not be objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. I thought it was pretty clear that we were referring to the Croatian media, both written media as well as the television media at this stage, and we were referring specifically to the period 1992 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the media -- the media is independent. They may be giving their spin to it or their analysis. That's one thing. Now, is it -- is she reading what the media is saying that officials are saying? Is it an official media source? What is it? It's as if I'm reading what The New York Times is saying and attributing that to the Bush administration, which nothing could be further from the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, when you talk about the Croatian media, I cannot establish a distinction between the media in Zagreb, in Croatian media they were operating out of Mostar. There is some degree of ambiguity here. In addition, your international correspondents, who were they, the ones you met in Mostar? "The media" is a very broad term. Can you perhaps give us details about the people you met and about your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the names of all the colleagues and -- but -- well, I was meeting pretty much of them, and what the media comes of course you are listening the news and looking TV if you are in a place where you can do it, but let's say I'm pretty many -- British journalists because the Brits were very active. And then when I was talking very often was a Spanish one with a German name. I have forgotten his name, but he was writing for biggest newspaper in Spain and got even some kind of journalistic prize. He was also making books. He was a very aware -- aware of the things. And I met several German ones. Not only Erich. Austrian ones from Austrian TV and from the newspaper Die Presse. And also from Kurier, but he was an idiot so I don't refer to him. And many others. But I have somewhere cards of the most of them, but after so many years journalists you have met sometimes -- they are very deep in my memory and I cannot pick them so quickly out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian media you mentioned, in Mostar did you meet journalists or journalists coming from Zagreb, people who were actually doing their job, or were you just listening to television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met some Croat journalists. They were quite active also, in Mostar especially, and I met also some Slovenian journalists sometime, one of my good -- which I was meeting often was got killed in Sarajevo. And then one I was talking with was a Slovenia. His name was Ervin. And so, yes, there was Croatian journalists, but I was also when I was in Croatian side, listening to radio news, or looking TV news, and reading some newspaper like Nedeljna Dalmacija which was not following government. Nedeljna Dalmacija was the freest newspaper in Croatia, and then Vjesnik which was more near government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may follow up on that. The television that you were watching, Croatian or in the context of Croatian media, which television stations were you following?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: The official ones. They were clearly in government hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, returning to the original question then, from these media could you gauge the line of reporting being followed with regard to the conflict between the Bosnian Croats or Herzegovinian Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, of course you could see it, because -- because media had -- has in a -- in a state which is not -- well, let's say in a state-owned or state near -- government near media always has a certain role, and so you could see from this media very well. For instance, in the beginning of war, already before, the media was very Muslim friendly, and Croatia was very Muslim friendly. It is true that they took hundred thousands of Muslim refugees. Also Croat refugees, but Muslim refugees. It's true. But then you could see that the policy is turning. Up after January '93, after Vance-Owen Plan, it was suddenly talking about fundamentalists and about a danger of Islamic republic, about Islamic Republic of Bosnia. So it was suddenly leading the opinion towards -- against Muslims. And then in the end of '93, beginning of '94 when they again started to do their common state, suddenly it was again friendly to Muslims. It means that you could -- it was like a wave. You could -- the Croatian attitude was corresponding what was happening in -- in this Croat-Muslim relation in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. But of course it's clear that -- that Croatian feelings were on Croatian side, but on the other side it was systematically leading our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in your context during the same period that we've been referring to your analysis of the Croatian press and television that you've given, were you -- could you comment or are you in a position to comment regarding your contacts with HVO officials and people you interviewed? How does -- how did that correspond to the views being presented on through the press and through the television?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Where is the nexus between the previous question and the answer - and of course journalists are free to comment however they wish - and this particular question the way it assumes facts that are certainly not in evidence? If he could lay a foundation, because now the assumption is, the assumption built into this question is that HVO or officials from Herceg-Bosna somehow influencing the -- the media in Croatia, which is why the Croatian media is reporting the way it does. One has nothing to do with the other. And I don't see, first of all, what the Croatian media has anything to do with -- with a particular indictment. Now, if that could be explained to me I would welcome, you know, perhaps more questions, but until we have some sort of a nexus and where we're going, it might be interesting, it might be prejudicial, but it's certainly not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, now to understand the question, you were a witness because you were present in the area and in Western Mostar. So you met a number of people. You witness a number of facts, and you were in contact with a number of people. The question which has been put to you now by the Prosecution and which has been challenged by Defence counsel is this: How did you see things? You wrote articles. You had interviews. Now your own view of the situation based on what you saw and based on what you heard in the Croatian media, did you share that same opinion or was it a different view you had, and if your view was different in what way was it different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, firstly, I would like to -- Mr. Defender, that I don't think that anybody is thinking that Herceg-Bosna is leading Croatian media. I think that -- that Croatia was very well aware what was happening in Herceg-Bosna, and the question to me was always how much is Croatian government involved in the happenings in Herceg-Bosna? Is the Herceg-Bosna leadership the highest, or is there still a higher level sitting in Zagreb? But it's not relevant at the moment, because this higher level is already in -- in graveyard. But anyway -- and in this meaning, this media was very interesting because it was exactly corresponding what was happening in Herceg-Bosna on the view of Croats and on behalf of Croats and repeating the propaganda of Islamic state and Muslim danger and telling from Middle Ages how the Croatia was always the bulwark against Muslims and fighting for Christianity, and these articles really were appearing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we can turn -- return, finally, to a document which we have looked at previously, and this is Exhibit 8575. Exhibit 8575. And this is the analysis that you made entitled "The Croats are sitting on three chairs." Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first page of the English version, right at the bottom it says, and this returns to the old question of the ultimatum, it says: "In April, the president of the self-proclaimed Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban imposed an ultimatum on the predominantly Muslim Bosnian army." Can you very briefly just comment on what basis you said Mate Boban imposed this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well -- well, I have to look at the German version to see what is about. Anyway, it was the 3rd of -- 3rd of April when according to all these previous press reports Boban made this ultimatum, and it was written to name of Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to the second page of this English version, and the second paragraph. It says: "The highest command of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban -- President Mate Boban and HVO President Jadranko Prlic ..." On what basis did you refer to them as the highest command of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, Mate Boban was the leader of Herceg-Bosna. He was the president. And Mr. Prlic was the leader of armed forces, and so in the wartime I think that the leader of armed forces is a very, very high leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And about Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we just go on in that sentence, it says that: Mr. Boban and Mr. Prlic are being more prudent in its statements, or the highest command is being most prudent. "Both of them are saying beautiful words about all groups of people living together and try to put the blame on the Muslims ..." Now, with regard to Mr. Prlic, on what basis did you write this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: On the basis of an interview where he was talking about, We don't have any problems living together with Muslims and so on. It means that -- that this higher level was talking more beautiful but in the middle -- middle level like it was more brutal. They were talking more direct. Let's say that they were not as good politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you recall on what basis you said the same of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I never interviewed Mr. Boban, but I was reading several interviews which other people had made. I was sometimes behind his door in Grude, but it never opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you recall whose interviews with Mr. Boban you read, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Anyway, Erich Rathfelder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] In order to be able to prepare for the defence, I'd like them to define the names, the middle levels with the names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you answer that question just put to you by Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean middle level -- middle level. The press officer, for instance, in Tomislavgrad Veso Vegar, and these persons with the -- and also I would count Dario Kordic to this middle level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, at the end of that paragraph there's a sentence: "In reality these gentlemen are the architects of ethnic cleansing." On what basis did you say this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: I say that on that basis, that they were trying to tell that it was some local commandants which were not obeying the orders from the centres and they were making a kind of solo dancing. But it is a very funny thing that it occurred everywhere in Central Bosnia at the same time, about 5.00 in the morning, 16th of April, but how they get so this obeyed in the same moment. There must be a higher order. And this opinion was publicly told also from Colonel Bob Stewart who was present when that all happened. Even they were a little bit sleeping, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, just related to which we touched upon earlier, in the next paragraph, second line, it says: "There have been rumours for a long time already about the secret trips to Pale from Boban to Karadzic. Jadranko Prlic did not deny these secret contacts." Just for the record then, on what did you -- on what did you base that entry?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Well, I had some information that it was not the only trip through Pale what Mr. Prlic was -- was telling, but -- but anyway, one of the basement was also this that he told, that Boban had been in Pale, but there were also others who told that it has happened several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, if we can turn to page 3 of the English version, and the second paragraph from the bottom which starts with "The core of the problem is that ... " Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, madam, this paragraph states that "The core of the problem is that the Croatian leadership cannot decide what kind of Croatia to strive for," and then three options or three -- let's call them options are given. "Officially, the aim is an independent Croatia with the current borders which is called Little Croatia," and then you refer, "In practice however Western Herzegovina is already annexed to Croatia. Especially the supporters of Mate Boban strive for this ethnically-cleansed Smaller Croatia. And then, however, there is a still a third version, Great Croatia up to the Drina." Is this your own categorisation or on what basis did you write this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It is, of course, my own -- my categorisation, but I think that I'm not alone -- alone in this -- this thing. It is -- it was one option. It means that -- that Croatia as an independent state. It was -- anyway it was -- it was the aim and at that moment when I was writing that Croatia was not Croatia, because about one-third were under Serbian control. But then the other option was, of course, joining Herceg-Bosna to Croatia. It means that they make an ethnically pure bigger Croatia. And there were some indications which were talking to this direction, and I'm not now going to so far as Ante Pavelic, which was also from Herzegovina, but let's say that in Croatian government were very many Herzegovinians, and -- and then it came even so far later that Herzegovina -- Herzegovina Croats could vote for -- in Croatian parliamentary election and for them were reserved even a certain amount of places. It means that there was not only rumours of -- of my analysis from smaller or Greater Croatia. It was -- it was worked in direction of it or how you can -- I have never before heard that in parliament are representatives from neighbouring country, for instance. That was not at that moment realised, but it tells that it's not -- it's not taken from the air this analysis. And in the third one, the Great Croatia, the Drina. This is the historical. This is the historical. There are some other persons as Paraga were wanting. It means some kind of federation with -- with Muslims, and of course, Serbs. They wanted to cleanse over the Drina River. And this is based on history. It means in the Austro-Hungarian time, but it's very interesting to notice that the very moderate Muslim leader Lagumdzija told me, I think in February 1993, that they are ready. They could make a federal state with Croatia. So it was -- it would have been possible, but Serbs had -- would have never said yes to that kind of option, but these options, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could I just make certain or check what you had said. Did I understand correctly that what you had said that Herzegovinian Croats had representation in the parliament of the republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Yeah, they had, but I don't remember now when they got it, but they had, and it was of course -- it was very funny. It was also still after the war. I think that this constitution is now changed, but it was -- it was. So it means that there was some kind of attempts to unificate Herceg-Bosna with Croatia. And you have to remember if you take the ethnical map, Herceg-Bosna is the most Croatian area in the whole Croatian-inhabited areas. There's -- in Grude there is, I think, 98 per cent or how much it was Croats. The only area in Croatia which was that Croat was Varazdin. All other places they had some kind of minority. So it was -- and I think that that was also was what Mr. Prlic meant when he told that Herzegovina is the heart of Croatia or more Croat as Croatia. It is really the purest Croatian populated area in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, if we can just turn the page to page 4 of this English transcript. And if we look at the second last paragraph. It says: "The splitting up of Bosnia is no new idea. Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic have already negotiated about that before the war." What are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: That's the meeting in Karadjordjevo. But I would say to that that knowing Milosevic a little bit he was a very clever guy. I don't think that -- that he was honest. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how much of this speculation the Trial Chamber is going to put up with. We've now -- it's been going on for some time. I've tried to be patient. If this witness is being asked to be an expert in certain areas, then she should be disclosed under Rule 94 bis. It's not right for her to be expressing these opinions without any notice to the Defence. This goes way beyond her statement and it's completely -- it's completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't pursue that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I have only one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a follow-up question. This famous document which Mr. Kruger is examining with you, on page 3 you talk about Mr. Paraga, and you expand on this and come up with a theory whereby the person in question was in favour of a confederation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that he was against the HVO, and you mentioned that he had been killed in November, that he had a private army. What do you base this on when you are writing about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that Paraga was killed. It was the Herzegovinian leadership of HOS. But he had the private army, HOS, and it was, of course, a kind of concurrence to HVO and it had a totally different ideology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in what way was that ideology totally different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted Great -- Great Croatia together with Muslims. He wanted to annex Bosnia to Croatia. And that was never the aim of HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your opinion Mr. Paraga wanted Bosnia to be annexed to Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which would have created a Greater Croatia. And you say that that was not what the HVO wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Because HVO didn't want the Muslims in the same state. They were talking about fundamentalistic danger and that kind of things. Even in this Prlic interview is -- is the word towards me, "Do you want an Islamic state?" And that was the difference. But in this Paraga ideology, which I know very well, there was a one thing. The Serbs would have been then kicked out because Serbs he didn't want to have in that Bosnia. He wanted to very Great Bosnia with Muslims but without Serbs. And HVO was cooperating very well with Serbs, but they were -- had this fundamentalistic card at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just checking something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: May we just for clarity, if I may ask you to just ask exactly what was the difference between the -- what you referred to as the Paraga ideology and then the HVO view?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: Paraga ideology was not that ethnical. It was not that ethnical pure. It was not that Croatian. For him were also -- he was also thinking Muslims. He was -- his thinking -- way of thinking were more historical, because if you go to the time before and let's say to -- before 1918, Bosnia and Croatia, they were both actually belonging to Hungary, and -- and they -- and he was thinking on this historical terms, but HVO were more thinking joining all the Croats in the same state. Exactly what the Serbs were -- the idea of Greater Serbia was to join all Serbs to the same state. It was everywhere published. And the HV ideology was about the same but on Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, I just want to ask you one last aspect. Earlier there had been reference to what Mr. Erich Rathfelder told you Mr. Prlic had told him after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: After the -- is sorry. After the grounding of federation between Croats and Muslims, after that peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: First peace before Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what Mr. Prlic told Mr. Rathfelder, to what period did that relate?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI
utterances.text: It relates on this -- this April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what did he tell Mr. Rathfelder --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. There was an objection, and it's common courtesy and rather professional to first ask for permission from the Court. Now that the question is phrased differently or laid a foundation, if he may go to -- revisit that area, but there was an objection. The objection was sustained. The gentleman moved on.
